Chapter 04

One file to configure everything

SvelteKit 3 keeps its whole configuration inside the Vite plugin. This chapter reads vite.config.ts top to bottom: plugin order, mdsvex as a preprocessor, per-file compiler options for the custom element, the inspector, the adapter, remote functions and the three namespaces called experimental, tracing, prerendering, the Content Security Policy, versioning and preloads in a header, Paraglide, and the two test projects — then tsconfig.json, and the options this project leaves at their defaults.

By the end of this chapter

Read a SvelteKit 3 config with three preprocessors and plugins in it and know what every line is for, including why order matters twice, and say which TypeScript options belong to SvelteKit and which to you.

There is no svelte.config.js. SvelteKit 3 moved every option into the sveltekit() plugin call, and this project feels that change more than the earlier ones did, because three of the tools it uses *used* to be configured through that file: mdsvex was a preprocessor listed there, @sveltejs/package read it for aliases, and every guide on the internet still says so. Here is where they go now.

defineConfig comes from vitest/config rather than vite, so the test block at the bottom type-checks; loadEnv still comes from Vite because Vitest does not re-export it. The config is a function because it reads the environment before the build starts: paths.origin is the value adapter-node bakes into the server, and it is read from PUBLIC_ORIGIN here and validated by src/env.ts (chapter 15) as static: true so the same value reaches Better Auth. relative: false beside it is a link decision, not a deployment one: every internal link goes through href(), and with SvelteKit’s default a server render’s links came out as whole URLs at the build’s origin. Chapter 25 tells that story where the links are written.

enhancedImages() must come before sveltekit(). It is a preprocessor that rewrites <enhanced:img> into a <picture> element, and the Svelte compiler has to see the rewritten markup, not the original. Put it second and the build fails with an unhelpful message about an unknown element. The other ordering rule is at the bottom of the plugin list, and it is the opposite way round.

Markdown components and a folder of custom elements

Two per-file behaviours. preprocess and extensions are what make a .svx file a component: mdsvex runs first, turns Markdown into markup and frontmatter into a metadata export, and the compiler takes it from there; extensions tells SvelteKit that .svx files under src/routes and in imports are components too. Chapter 36 writes the guides that use it.

dynamicCompileOptions is newer and subtler: a function called once per file, returning compiler options for that file only. The custom element in src/lib/embed has to be compiled with customElement: true — a different output altogether, a class the browser can register as an element, with a shadow root — and nothing else in the project may be, which is why the test is the path src/lib/embed and not any folder called embed: the frame page lives in src/routes/embed, and the looser test once compiled it as a custom element too, so its styles went into a shadow root that never existed. The environment.name === "client" guard is the part people miss: the server build compiles the same file, and a custom element has no server-rendered form, so the server gets a plain component it never renders. Chapter 38 builds the element.

The compiler options

runes is a function so that a dependency written in Svelte 4 style keeps compiling — several libraries in this project ship .svelte files, and the compiler decides per file. experimental.async is the one that changes how you write components: await at the top level of a <script>, inside $derived, and directly in markup, with <svelte:boundary> and its pending snippet to catch the wait. This project has more of it than any before: the globe is an await import() in markup, the explore page and the new-trip form await places() at the top of their scripts — one prerendered list, waited for once, before the first render — and opening a trip is {const initial = $derived(await tripBySlug(slug))} on the page.

What the compiled output asks of a browser: Svelte’s own documentation gives Chrome and Edge 87, Firefox 83 and Safari 14 — a Baseline target of 2020 — for Svelte itself, with a few exceptions it lists by feature, two of which this project uses: $state.snapshot needs Chrome 98, Firefox 94 or Safari 15.4 (the library’s toJSON, ch. 07), and flip from svelte/animate needs Firefox 126 (the itinerary’s reordering, ch. 27). The table covers Svelte, not SvelteKit, the libraries or your own code; MapLibre’s WebGL and the CSS this project writes — light-dark() among it — ask for newer browsers than that, and together they set the real floor — in Firefox it is flip, at 126, higher than light-dark()’s 120.

The comment says it: inspector is not SvelteKit’s. The plugin passes any option it does not own to vite-plugin-svelte — the JSDoc on sveltekit() puts it as “Any options that don’t belong to SvelteKit are passed through to vite-plugin-svelte, so you can set options like inspector here too” — and vite-plugin-svelte documents the inspector as “unset for dev, always false for build”. Setting it switches it on in the dev server and costs a production build nothing. Of its options, toggleKeyCombo defaults to alt-x, and the plugin advises combinations of modifiers alone, so that turning it on can never type into an input. The default is kept anyway: every pair of modifiers is already somebody’s shortcut — Ctrl+Shift and Alt+Shift switch keyboard layouts on Windows — and the inspector only exists in the dev server. showToggleButton is always, active (the default) or never.

The adapter, remote functions, and one experiment left off

precompress matters more here than in any earlier project: MapLibre and three.js are the two largest chunks any of the eight has shipped, and writing .br and .gz beside them at build time means the server never compresses them per request. remoteFunctions is the switch for everything in chapters 17–20. forkPreloads stays off on the evidence of three projects; the comment says what would turn it on, which is how a decision that might change should be recorded.

The word experimental appears twice in this file, and it belongs to three projects. compilerOptions.experimental.async is Svelte’s: await in components, a flag the documentation says “will be removed in Svelte 6”. The top-level experimental is SvelteKit’s — remoteFunctions and forkPreloads — and it is shared: SvelteKit’s types define it as vite-plugin-svelte’s experimental options plus its own, and the JSDoc says “SvelteKit reads its own flags and forwards the rest”. The experimental add-on from ch. 03 writes both kinds in one line, sv add experimental="features:async,remoteFunctions", which is also its default.

forkPreloads is the one that ties them together. Svelte 5.42 added fork(), which “makes it possible to run await expressions that you *expect* to happen in the near future” — start the work a state change would cause, then commit() it if the change happens or discard() it if it does not. The documentation says it is “mainly intended for frameworks like SvelteKit to implement preloading when (for example) users signal an intent to navigate”, and forkPreloads is SvelteKit doing exactly that on a hovered link. Two caveats come with async mode, both in its documentation: the details “are subject to breaking changes outside of a semver major release”, and effects run in a slightly different order — block effects such as {#if} and {#each} now run before an $effect.pre in the same component. Nothing in this project depends on that order; the end-to-end suite is what would notice if something did.

tracing.server was experimental in SvelteKit 2 and is not in 3; it makes every handle, load, form action and remote function an OpenTelemetry span, and src/instrumentation.server.ts — loaded before any application code, with nothing to switch on — is where the exporter lives. Chapter 37 reads the spans back on the diagnostics page. The two explicit 'fail' values restate the default, so that the intent is in the file: a broken link or a missing #id on a prerendered page fails the build, which is the only time you want to find out. The other three handlers — handleEntryGeneratorMismatch, handleUnseenRoutes and handleInvalidUrl — also default to 'fail'. The options left out keep their defaults too: entries is ["*"], every route without a required parameter; crawl is true, so the build follows links from there, which is how /de/guides and /pt-br/guides are found — through the language switcher’s links, with no entry of their own; and concurrency is 1, which is right for pages whose content is in the repository rather than behind a network.

The Content Security Policy

The comment above the directives is the chapter. Two things to add. mode: "auto" means hashes on prerendered pages and nonces on dynamic ones — and a nonce is filled in per request, which is why the theme boot script in app.html is allowed by its hash and carries no nonce attribute: SvelteKit refuses to prerender a template that still contains %sveltekit.nonce%, and the guides are prerendered. themeBootHash() at the bottom of the file reads the script out of app.html and hashes it, so the two cannot drift.

connect-src "self" with no tile server is a real constraint accepted on purpose: the map cannot fetch tiles from anybody, so it is built from a bundled atlas (chapter 29). If you add a tile provider, this is the line that changes, and the CSP will tell you so in the console before anything else does.

Versioning, so a deploy does not strand open tabs, and preloads in a header

version.name is the commit hash, computed by commitHash() below with a fallback to the package version, because a Docker build context has no .git. SvelteKit 3 notices a new version without asking: the current version rides on every data, remote and form response as an x-sveltekit-version header, and the client checks again whenever the tab regains focus or becomes visible. pollInterval is the fallback for a tab parked on one page, which is exactly what the trip page is — a live query delivers its changes over one long response, so no new headers arrive — and so it is a minute here rather than the default hour. When a new version is seen, updated.current in the root layout flips, a banner offers a reload, and the next navigation becomes a full page load so no chunk from the old build is ever requested. bundleStrategy: "split" is the default and is named here because chapter 38 builds the one thing that must *not* be split.

linkHeaderPreload moves a dynamically rendered page’s preloads out of the HTML and into a Link response header — the modules, the stylesheet, and the two fonts the preload hook in hooks.server.ts picks by source filename (ch. 46). The browser reads headers before the body, so it starts on them a little sooner; prerendered pages keep their <link> tags, because a file on disk has no headers to carry them. The option has existed since 3.0 and is off by default for the reason its documentation gives and the comment repeats: Nginx and Apache limit header sizes by default, and this header is not small — about 7.5 KB on the trip page, the page with the most to preload. A test in e2e/public.e2e.ts holds the header to its promise: /explore must answer with rel="modulepreload" and the Fraunces font in its Link header, and with no modulepreload left in its HTML.

Three plugins that are not SvelteKit

Paraglide is a Vite plugin in its own right: it watches messages/*.json, compiles them into src/lib/paraglide, and does so with a strategy list that is the order the locale is decided in. Chapter 21 is entirely about it. The phosphor plugin is the second ordering rule: it rewrites import { PlusIcon } from "phosphor-svelte" into a deep import so the dev server does not crawl a barrel of thousands of icons, and it must run *after* the Svelte compiler because it parses JavaScript. Put it first and it dies on the first <h1>. The third, bundleStats(), is this project’s own and runs only in a build: at the end of the browser build it writes down which modules went into which chunk, so that a script can hold the bundle to a budget afterwards. A chunk’s file name is a hash and changes with every edit; the bundler is the one place that knows what a chunk *is*. Chapter 45 is where that script runs, and why it exists.

The native addon, and the two test projects

Two Vitest projects in one config — and no extends line on either, because since Vitest 5 an inline project inherits the config that declares it, plugins and #lib included, unless it says extends: false: client runs *.svelte.test.ts in a real Chromium through Playwright, because the components under test need WebGL, pointer events and layout; server runs everything else in Node, one file at a time because SQLite has one writer. The optimizeDeps.include list is the fix for a real failure: the phosphor plugin rewrites imports during transform, after Vite’s dependency scan, so on a cold cache Vite discovered the icons mid-test, re-bundled, and reloaded the test inside itself. Naming them is what Vitest’s own warning asks for. Chapter 44 runs both projects.

The other file: tsconfig.json

"extends": "$app/tsconfig" is the line SvelteKit owns. svelte-kit sync writes that config into node_modules/$app/tsconfig.json every time it runs, with what a SvelteKit project needs: moduleResolution: "bundler", the DOM libraries, and rootDirs set to the project and .svelte-kit/types side by side — which is how import type { PageProps } from './$types' beside a route finds a file that lives in a generated folder. Four of its options are SvelteKit’s to set, and its documentation says overriding them “may cause things to break”: paths (derived from subpath imports; here it is empty, because bundler resolution reads imports from package.json itself), types (it must include $app/types, the generated module declarations), isolatedModules (“Vite compiles modules one at a time”) and verbatimModuleSyntax (“so that you can safely use type imports in .svelte files”). Everything in compilerOptions above is this project’s own strictness, each with the reason beside it.

The explicit include and exclude are required in SvelteKit 3, and the comment says what happens without them. One folder is excluded for a different reason: src/service-worker runs in a worker’s global scope, with caches and FetchEvent and no document, so it has a tsconfig of its own that extends $app/tsconfig/service-worker — the WebWorker library instead of the DOM — and pnpm run check checks it with a second program (ch. 39). erasableSyntaxOnly is the newest line: TypeScript refuses any syntax that cannot simply be deleted to leave JavaScript — enum, a namespace with values in it, a constructor parameter marked private — because the two places this project runs TypeScript without a compiler cannot run it either. Node 24 runs scripts/*.ts by stripping the types; Svelte 5 compiles a lang="ts" block the same way. (namespace App in src/app.d.ts is a declaration, types only, and stays.)

Why not vitePreprocess({ script: true }) instead

It is the other answer to the same question: run TypeScript through a real transpiler before Svelte sees it, and enums and parameter properties work in components. The integrations documentation names the cases for it — a project before Svelte 5, or “advanced TypeScript features that emit code” — and adds that otherwise “you probably don’t need to use vitePreprocess”. This project has neither case, and the flag is cheaper than the preprocessor in both directions: nothing extra runs on every component in the build, and the code stays runnable by every tool that strips types, Node’s included. One rule instead of a second compiler.

What this file leaves at its defaults

A config is also defined by what it does not say. These are the options a reader of other projects will meet, and why this one does not set them:

  • **files.*** — where SvelteKit looks for things, and the defaults are the names: src/routes, src/params, src/hooks.server, src/hooks.client, src/hooks (the universal hooks), src/service-worker, src/app.html and src/error.html. This project uses the defaults for every one it has — src/hooks.client.ts and src/params.ts among them — and a file with one of the other names, a src/service-worker folder or a src/error.html, would be picked up the same way. The option is deprecated in 3.0, with a workspace recommended instead, which is what packages/waypoint is.
  • moduleExtensions — [".js", ".ts"], the extensions treated as modules; nothing here needs another.
  • outDir — .svelte-kit, where SvelteKit writes generated types and build output (ch. 02).
  • env.dir — ".", the folder searched for .env files.
  • embedded — false. true attaches SvelteKit’s navigation listeners to the element that holds the app instead of window, for an app embedded in a larger page; Meridian’s embed is a frame and a custom element instead (ch. 38).
  • paths.base and paths.assets — empty: the app is served from the root of its origin, and its assets from the same origin. (paths.origin and paths.relative are set, at the top of the file.)
  • emitCss — vite-plugin-svelte’s, default true: component styles become virtual CSS files that Vite bundles, rather than being injected by JavaScript. Nothing here needs it changed.
  • prebundleSvelteLibraries — vite-plugin-svelte’s, “true for dev, false for build”: in the dev server, Svelte libraries are prebundled like any other dependency. The optimizeDeps.include list for the browser tests is the one place this project steps in.
  • hot — older guides set it; vite-plugin-svelte 7 has no such option. Hot reloading is Svelte 5’s own hmr compiler option, which the plugin turns on in the dev server unless Vite’s server.hmr is off.

Checkpoint

  • You can say which two plugins have ordering rules, which way round each goes, and why.
  • You can explain why the boot script is allowed by a hash and not a nonce, and what would break if it were the other way.
  • You know what dynamicCompileOptions is for and why it checks environment.name.
  • You can say which project owns each experimental flag in the file — Svelte, SvelteKit or vite-plugin-svelte.
  • You can say which four TypeScript options SvelteKit sets for you, and what erasableSyntaxOnly forbids and why.
